title: 'Tennessee Waltz' and Patti Page
summary: He explains how audience requests led to his Decca recording and how Patti Page's version overshadowed it.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: On some of them, a lot of people don't know I did this, "Tennessee Waltz". (laughter) Can you imagine me doing a waltz? Well, I went to do a session with Decca. I was, Avery, not Avery Parrish. Ace Harris was playing piano with me then. At the Savoy barroom, I used to do, late at night, I used to do waltzes cause this was my last hour. It was getting closing time. So, I used to point to different men when they wanted to play a tune. So, they'd just holler. I said give me an E flat, modulate to E flat or a G or something. Then, they'd would pick the tune up. We would just follow. So, everytime I'd point to Ace Harris, he would go into "Tennessee Waltz". Sometimes he'd have it too high because he sang it too. If it was too high, we used to laugh at him cause the "Tennessee Waltz" was a, he could do the tune but he'd never give up. He kept on changing the key until he got at a key that he

could sing it in.
So, after we started playing it and
we got it straight, people used to come up there.
Now, this was a medley. People used to come up
and say play that tune that you, about that
Tennessee thing you were talking about. So, they
were talking about the "Tennessee Waltz".
So, I took the tune out and made
a single out of it. And, we just played the
"Tennessee Waltz".
So, I go down to record at Decca.
They said well, what's you gonna do for your
sixth number. I said I'm gonna do "Tennessee
Waltz". They said Oh, no, no. Hawk, you ain't
never do no "Tennessee Waltz". Why don't you do
something, you know, like you been doing all the
time. They wanted me to do the swing thing like
"After Hours". I said the reason why I was
doing this is on account people kept requesting
this number.
So, they gave into me after a half
hour talk with them. So, this was one I had to
cup mute solo in it straight, you know, and
everything. It's like, it was like the original arrangement. I don't know if you ever heard mine cause Patti Pace did one not too long after that, you know?
But, that was my whole arrangement, all the stuff except the dub her voice.

Now, I met Patti Page's manager in Madison Square Garden. I went there for a hockey game, and he, his seat was right next to mine. And, he made himself know. He said, 'You are Erskine Hawkins?' I said yeah. He said, 'I'm Patti Page's manager. I'm the one that went over to Decca. I needed a tune for Patti Page's second number,' like she did a tune like 'Boogie Woogie Santa Claus'? No, 'The Little Doll In The Window' or something like that. They wanted another side.
So, Decca said why don't you take this? Hawkins just made this. Although my tune had started to move it a little bit, and they said make this, take this. So, he did, and they
did it and did the double voices and everything on it which was beautiful when she did it, you know. There's no question about that.

And, and so he told me the whole story right there, sitting there, and I said what. Then Patti, I met Patti Page later, and she told me how much she liked it. And, she used to give me a little credit on it.
But, there it was being played on the radio before my tune started getting on a little. Then, they covered it up with hers then.

So, they no heard me do no waltz before. You know? Because nobody would expect me to do a waltz. So Decca, after that, started putting it in magazines, 'the man who started it!' (Laughter) It was too late then. It was too late then. It was a smash for Patti Page.
